pages.x: Maintenance A monthly WordPress maintenance checklist A short, repeatable routine that keeps a WordPress site healthy, secure and fast. 15 August 2026 admin WordPress sites don’t look after themselves. A small amount of regular attention prevents most of the problems that otherwise appear at the worst possible moment. Every month Update WordPress core, plugins and themes, ideally after testing on staging. Confirm backups are running and that a recent one is stored off site. Remove plugins and themes that are no longer used. Review user accounts and remove anyone who no longer needs access. Check forms still send and that key pages load correctly. Every quarter Restore a backup to a staging site to prove it works. Look for broken links and missing images. Review page speed on the most important pages. Check that the PHP version is still supported by your host. Every year Renew domains and certificates, or confirm they renew automatically. Review hosting: is the plan still the right size? Audit content: archive or update pages that are out of date. Write it down Keep a simple log of what was updated and when. When something breaks, the log tells you what changed. pages.x: WordPress Security Backups are a security control When everything else fails, a good backup is how you recover. Here is what makes a backup strategy actually work. 9 October 2026 admin No security measure is perfect. Backups are what turn a disaster into an inconvenience, provided they are done well. Follow the 3-2-1 idea A common rule of thumb is three copies of your data, on two different types of storage, with one copy kept off site. For a website that usually means the live site, a copy with your host, and a copy somewhere independent of the host. Back up files and the database A WordPress site is both: uploads, themes and plugins live in files, while content and settings live in the database. A backup that misses either half will not restore a working site. Match frequency to change A site that publishes every day needs more frequent backups than a brochure site updated once a month. Consider how much work you could afford to lose and schedule accordingly. Keep backups long enough Some compromises go unnoticed for weeks. If you only keep the last few days of backups, every copy may already contain the problem. Keep a range of older restore points. Test restores Restore a backup to a staging site from time to time. It proves the backup works and that you know the process before you need it under pressure. Back to all posts More from the blog Three more articles, picked at random. pages.x: BRXProd & Bricks Builder notes that live where the work is Notes in BRXProd attach to the site, a page, an element or just you, so context stays with the thing it is about. 29 August 2026 admin Every project accumulates small pieces of knowledge: why a section is built a certain way, what the client asked to change, which element is waiting on copy. Usually that knowledge lives in someone’s head or a separate document. Four scopes BRXProd’s builder notes can be attached at four levels: Site : decisions that affect everything, such as type scale choices Page : what a page still needs before launch Element : a reminder on the exact block it concerns Personal : your own to-do list, visible only to you Ticking things off Notes can be marked done, grouped and reorganised, so they work as a lightweight checklist rather than a growing pile of comments. Handover without a handover document Because notes sit next to the work, the next person to open the page sees them in context. That makes handing a site to a colleague, or coming back to it months later, much less painful. Notes and agents Notes are also available as WordPress abilities. An agent can read the notes on a page before editing it, or leave a note explaining a change it made, which keeps people and automated work in the same conversation. pages.x: BRXProd & Bricks Client feedback without the email chain BRXProd's feedback desk keeps client comments on the page they're about, with statuses, assignees and review rounds. 7 September 2026 admin Client feedback often arrives as a long email with screenshots, half of which refer to an older version of the page. Matching each comment to the right element takes time, and things get missed. Feedback on the page itself With BRXProd’s Client Feedback, reviewers leave comments directly on the page or element they are talking about. Each item has a status, so it is always clear what is new, in progress, waiting on the client or approved. Internal and client-visible replies Replies can be visible to the client or kept internal. The team can discuss an item without the client seeing every back-and-forth, then reply once with an answer. Review rounds Feedback can be grouped into review rounds. A round gives a clear start and finish: everything raised in round one is dealt with before round two begins, and finished rounds stay on record. Sharing drafts and approving pages Draft pages can be shared with reviewers before they are public, and pages can be formally approved. Contributors and invites are managed from the same place, so access stays tidy. Where it helps most Small teams with several projects at once get the most from it: one place to see what every client has said, who is dealing with it, and what is still open. pages.x: Components Generic blocks, styled once Buttons take their look only from their own controls and the theme style. Cards are one generic block whatever they show. Buttons Every style and size comes from the Button element's controls; there is no button CSS anywhere on the site. Primary Secondary Light Dark Muted Info Success Warning Danger Size sm Size md Size lg Size xl Primary outline Secondary outline Cards One card-v2 block with an optional image. What changes is content, a Surface class, or a BRXProd utility. Default A plain card Kicker, title, text and a Button. The button sits at the bottom because the text grows, not because the button is styled. Open the carousel Line clamp Long text, three lines brxp-line-clamp with brxp-line-clamp--3 cuts this paragraph after three lines however long it gets. It keeps cards in a row the same height when the copy varies from a sentence to a short essay, which is exactly what happens once real content arrives. Clickable box + focus The whole card is the link Tab to it: brxp-focus-here draws the focus ring around the card, not just the title.

h: Scoops and flares in pure CSS
pages.x: Corners Scoops and flares in pure CSS BRXProd's corner utilities cut inverted corners with a mask and add outset flares with a pseudo-element. Inverted radius A mask scoops each corner into the element. Combine as many corners as you like; tune the size with --inverted-radius. brxp-inverted-radius-top-left-horizontal brxp-inverted-radius-top-right-horizontal brxp-inverted-radius-bottom-left-horizontal brxp-inverted-radius-bottom-right-horizontal All four corners at once Corners on images The same mask works on an image: put the corner classes on the Image element itself. brxp-inverted-radius-top-left-horizontal. Photo: Steven Spassov / Unsplash. brxp-inverted-radius-bottom-right-horizontal. Photo: Florian Klauer / Unsplash. All four inverted corners at once. Photo: Linh Nguyen / Unsplash. Outset radius A pseudo-element flares out of the corner into the parent. Here the tab's bottom-right corner curves into its panel; --outset-color matches the tab. brxp-outset-radius-bottom-right-horizontal The panel joins the tab without a seam. Use at most two outset classes per element: one -horizontal (::before) and one -vertical (::after).

pages.x: BRXProd & Bricks GSAP motion without the copy-paste mess How BRXProd's GSAP Loader and the GSAP Prompt Library keep animation code organised, one effect per snippet. 3 October 2026 admin GSAP makes ambitious animation possible, but the code tends to sprawl: script tags pasted into several places, plugins loaded on every page, effects nobody remembers adding. One loader BRXProd’s GSAP Loader snippet is the single place GSAP and its plugins are loaded. You uncomment the plugins a site actually uses and nothing else is pulled in. There are no stray CDN tags scattered through pages. A library of effects The GSAP Prompt Library at gsap.brxprod.com catalogues well over a hundred effects for text, UI, overlays, forms, media, cursors, SVG and scroll. Each one has a description, the plugins it needs, sample code and the HTML it expects. Starting from a tested effect is faster than writing one from scratch. One snippet per effect Each effect goes in its own snippet, named after it. If a hover lift feels too much, you switch that snippet off; the rest of the site’s motion is untouched. Respecting reduced motion The library’s effects use GSAP’s matchMedia to respect the visitor’s reduced-motion preference: continuous motion stops and hover feedback becomes instant. Accessibility is part of the recipe rather than an afterthought. The Motion page on this site shows four of these effects, each running from its own snippet. pages.x: Maintenance Keeping a WordPress site fast over time Sites tend to slow down as they grow. These habits keep performance from quietly drifting. 20 September 2026 admin A new site is usually quick. Over months, new plugins, larger images and growing databases chip away at that speed until visitors start to notice. Images Images are often the heaviest part of a page. Upload them at sensible dimensions, use modern formats where your setup supports them, and let WordPress serve appropriately sized versions. Caching Page caching serves pre-built pages instead of rebuilding them for every visitor. Many hosts include it; otherwise a caching plugin does the job. Remember to clear the cache after significant changes. Plugins Each plugin can add scripts, styles and database queries. Review the plugin list regularly and remove anything that isn’t pulling its weight. Database housekeeping Post revisions, spam comments and expired temporary data accumulate. Clean them up periodically, and consider limiting how many revisions are kept. Measure, don’t guess Test the same few pages with the same tool every so often and note the results. A steady record makes it obvious when something has slowed the site down, and roughly when it happened. Back to all posts More from the blog Three more articles, picked at random. pages.x: BRXProd & Bricks Layout Rails: stop fighting max-width Named grid lines replace the usual wrapper-and-max-width dance. Here is how BRXProd's rails work and why they make layouts easier to change. 11 August 2026 admin Most page builders give you one tool for width: a container with a max-width. Anything wider or narrower means another wrapper, a negative margin, or a one-off class. Layout Rails takes a different approach. One grid, five named rails Put brxp-rails on a section and it becomes a grid with named lines: full, layout, breakout, wide and content, each with a start and an end. Every direct child sits on the content rail by default. pages.x: WordPress Security Logins, roles and two-factor authentication The login screen is the front door of a WordPress site. These measures make it much harder to walk through uninvited. 11 September 2026 admin Attackers rarely need a clever exploit if they can simply log in. Protecting accounts is one of the most effective security steps you can take. Two-factor authentication for administrators With two-factor authentication, a stolen password is not enough on its own. Use an authenticator app or security key rather than SMS where possible, and require it for every account that can install plugins or change settings. Unique usernames and passwords Avoid obvious usernames such as “admin” and never reuse passwords across sites. A password manager makes long, unique passwords practical. Limit login attempts Repeated failed logins are a sign of automated guessing. Limiting attempts, or protecting the login with a firewall, slows these attacks to the point of uselessness. Review user accounts regularly People leave projects; contractors finish their work. Remove accounts that are no longer needed and downgrade roles that are higher than necessary. An old administrator account is an easy target. Application passwords and API access Integrations often use application passwords or API tokens. Give each integration its own credential so it can be revoked without affecting anything else, and remove credentials for tools you no longer use. pages.x: WordPress Security Plugins and themes: your biggest attack surface Every plugin adds code that can contain vulnerabilities. Here is how to keep your plugin list lean and trustworthy. 25 August 2026 admin WordPress core receives a lot of scrutiny. Plugins and themes vary much more in quality, and together they usually make up most of the code running on a site. Fewer plugins, less risk Every active plugin is code that runs on your server. Before installing one, ask whether the feature is needed, whether a plugin you already use covers it, or whether a small snippet would do. Signs a plugin is worth trusting recent updates and a clear changelog a developer or company with a track record compatibility with the current WordPress version responsive support and a public way to report security issues Remove, don’t just deactivate A deactivated plugin’s files still sit on the server. If you are not using a plugin, delete it. The same goes for themes: keep the active theme, perhaps one default theme as a fallback, and remove the rest. Watch for abandoned plugins Plugins that stop receiving updates become riskier over time. Keep an eye out for plugins that haven’t been updated in a long while and plan replacements before a vulnerability forces the issue. Nulled software Pirated copies of premium plugins and themes frequently contain backdoors. The money saved is rarely worth cleaning up a compromised site. pages.x: Static Sites Static or dynamic WordPress? A decision guide A few questions that help decide whether a site should stay dynamic, go static, or use a hybrid of both. 20 October 2026 admin There is no universally right answer, but a few questions usually make the choice clear. Does the site change per visitor? Shops, memberships, learning platforms and dashboards show different content to different people. They are natural dynamic sites. Brochure sites, portfolios, documentation and many blogs show the same pages to everyone, which suits static delivery. How often does content change? Daily updates across many pages make rebuild times and publishing workflows more important. A site updated weekly or monthly barely notices them. Which features need a server? List the interactive features: forms, search, comments, bookings. For each, decide whether a service can provide it on a static site or whether it needs WordPress running for visitors. Who edits the site? If editors are comfortable in WordPress, keeping WordPress as the private editing environment and publishing a static copy can give them a familiar workflow with static delivery. A hybrid is often the answer Many sites keep WordPress for editing and dynamic sections while serving most pages statically or from a full-page cache. Start from what visitors need, then choose the delivery that serves it with the least risk and maintenance. Back to all posts More from the blog Three more articles, picked at random. pages.x: Static Sites Static websites: what ‘static’ really means A static site serves ready-made files instead of building each page on request. Here is what that means in practice. 8 August 2026 admin “Static” sounds like a site that never changes. That’s not quite it. A static site can be updated as often as you like; what is static is how pages are delivered. Dynamic delivery A typical WordPress page is built on request: the server runs PHP, queries the database and assembles HTML for each visitor, unless a cache steps in. Static delivery A static site generates its pages ahead of time. The server, or a content delivery network, simply hands out files: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images. There is no database query and no PHP running when a visitor arrives. Where the content comes from Static sites can be produced in several ways: written by hand or with a static site generator from text files exported from a CMS such as WordPress, which remains the editing environment built from a headless CMS through an API Static is not the same as simple Static pages can include rich interactivity in the browser, and services can provide search, forms and comments. The difference is where the work happens: at build time and in the visitor’s browser, rather than on your server for each request. pages.x: Static Sites The cons of static sites Static sites trade some convenience for speed and security. Know the trade-offs before you switch. 29 September 2026 admin Static sites aren’t the right fit for everything. Their strengths come from removing server-side work, and some features depend on exactly that work. Dynamic features need extra services Anything that responds to a visitor on the server, such as forms, site search, comments, memberships or shopping carts, needs a third-party service, a serverless function or a hybrid setup. Each adds cost and another account to manage. Changes need a rebuild When content changes, pages have to be regenerated and published. For a small site that’s quick; for a large site, rebuild times and publishing workflows need planning. Personalisation is harder Showing different content per visitor, such as logged-in dashboards or location-based content, is natural for a dynamic site and awkward for a static one. Editors may notice the difference If the static site is exported from a CMS, editors still work in the CMS, but there is an extra publish step and a short delay before changes appear. Preview needs thought too. Some plugins won’t work Plugins that rely on server-side processing for visitors won’t function on the static copy. A static setup works best when you know which features you need and plan for each one. Back to all posts More from the blog Three more articles, picked at random. For the right kind of site, the benefits are substantial. Speed Serving a ready-made file is about the least work a server can do. A smaller attack surface With no PHP or database exposed to the public, many common attacks simply have nothing to target. There is no login page on the public site and no plugins running for visitors. Low-cost, resilient hosting Static files can be hosted cheaply, sometimes for free, and they cope well with sudden traffic spikes. A popular post doesn’t need a bigger server. pages.x: WordPress Security The WordPress security basics that actually matter Most WordPress compromises come from a few predictable gaps. Close these first before reaching for anything exotic. 6 August 2026 admin WordPress security advice can feel endless. In practice, most compromised sites share a handful of causes, and fixing those removes most of the risk. Keep everything updated Outdated plugins and themes are the most common way in. Updates often contain security fixes, and once a fix is public, attackers know exactly what to look for on sites that haven’t applied it. Use strong, unique passwords and two-factor authentication Reused passwords leaked from other services are tried against WordPress logins constantly. A password manager and two-factor authentication on every administrator account stop most of these attempts. Give people only the access they need Not everyone needs to be an administrator. Editors, authors and contributors exist for a reason, and fewer administrator accounts means fewer accounts worth stealing. Choose plugins carefully Install plugins from reputable sources, check that they are actively maintained, and remove the ones you no longer use. Never install “nulled” copies of paid plugins; they are a common way of spreading malware. Have backups you have tested A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan. Keep copies off the server and practise restoring one. Use HTTPS everywhere HTTPS protects logins and form data in transit. It is now standard and usually free through your host. None of this is glamorous, but it is where the real protection comes from. Back to all posts More from the blog Three more articles, picked at random. pages.x: Maintenance Updating safely with a staging site Updates keep a site secure, but they occasionally break things. A staging site lets you find out before your visitors do. 2 September 2026 admin Skipping updates is risky; applying them blindly to a live site is risky too. A staging site is the middle path. What a staging site is A staging site is a private copy of your live site on the same kind of server. Many hosts can create one in a few clicks, and some can push changes back to live when you are happy. A simple update routine Refresh staging from the live site so it matches current content. Apply updates on staging, one group at a time. Check the pages that matter most: home, key landing pages, forms, checkout if you have one. Look at the browser console and the site’s error log for new warnings. Apply the same updates to live, then do a quick check there too. When an update breaks something Because you found it on staging, the live site is unaffected. Check the plugin’s changelog and support forum, roll back that update on staging, and decide whether to wait for a fix or replace the plugin. Security updates are urgent For updates that fix an actively exploited vulnerability, the risk of waiting can outweigh the risk of a quick update. Apply them promptly, with a fresh backup in hand. pages.x: Maintenance Uptime, logs and knowing when something breaks The worst way to find out your site is down is from a customer. Monitoring tells you first. 14 October 2026 admin Problems are much easier to fix when you know about them early. A little monitoring goes a long way. Uptime monitoring An uptime monitor checks your site every few minutes from outside and alerts you if it stops responding. Many services offer a free tier that is plenty for small sites. Check more than the home page A site can load its home page while its contact form or checkout is broken. Where your monitoring allows, check a key page or look for specific text on it. Read the error log PHP errors and warnings are written to a log on the server. A sudden increase after an update is an early sign that something is wrong, often before anything visibly breaks. Watch certificate and domain expiry An expired certificate or domain takes a site offline as surely as a server failure. Make sure renewals are automatic and that reminders go to an address someone actually reads. Decide who responds Alerts are only useful if someone acts on them. Agree who receives them and what they should do first, such as checking the host’s status page and the most recent change. Back to all posts More from the blog Three more articles, picked at random. pages.x: BRXProd & Bricks What Bricks Productivity adds to Bricks Builder A tour of the layer BRXProd puts on top of Bricks: layout rails, Surfaces, corner utilities, a generated Style Guide, snippets, notes and client feedback. 2 August 2026 admin Bricks Builder is fast on its own. Bricks Productivity (BRXProd) is about the work around the builder: the decisions you make on every project, the conventions you repeat, and the conversations with clients that usually happen somewhere else. A system, not a pile of utilities BRXProd installs a small set of locked classes and variables that work together: Layout Rails : a grid with named lines, so an element picks its width by naming a rail. Surfaces : four colour sets that paint panels and the page itself. Corner utilities : inverted and outset radius without images. Basic utilities : line clamps, clickable boxes, focus rings and spacing resets. Because the classes are locked, they behave the same on every site. You compose them with your own BEM classes instead of rewriting the same CSS each time. A Style Guide you don’t have to maintain by hand BRXProd can generate a Style Guide page from the site’s real tokens. When the palette or type scale changes, regenerating the page shows the new values, so the guide never drifts from the design system. Work that leaves the builder less often Builder notes, client feedback and code snippets all live inside WordPress. Notes attach to a page or an element; feedback has statuses, assignees and review rounds; snippets have names and on/off switches. Fewer things live in email threads and sticky notes. Built for people and agents Many of these features are exposed as WordPress abilities, which an AI agent can call with the same permissions you set. Each group can be switched on or off in the plugin’s settings, so you decide what an agent is allowed to touch. The rest of this series looks at each piece in turn.
